transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-08   Time: 15:00 UTC   Duration: ~55min
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Tara (Redwood CSM), Dr. Priya Kapoor (Aquifer), Jared Holt (Aquifer Infra), Sofia Martinez (Aquifer CISO), Evan Rivers (Aquifer Product)

[00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for squeezing us in. Quick roll call and then we'll jump into your current workload and cost constraints.
[00:12] Priya: Hi, Priya here. We're excited. Kind of juggling a couple things, mostly inference for variant calling and internal docs summarization.
[00:20] Jared: Jared, infra. We run most pipelines on-prem but have some cloud pockets, so residency matters.
[00:28] Sofia: Sofia, security. I'll be listening for SSO/KMS/audit stuff.
[00:33] Liam (SE): Hey all. Quick note — I'll dig into batching and KV cache questions, and give some back-of-envelope numbers.
[00:40] Maya: Great. Priya could you frame the traffic profile? average prompt length, percent of long-seq requests?
[00:48] Priya: Yeah. So roughly 70% are short queries — 30-150 tokens, think search/rerank and short summaries. The other 30% are longer analysis jobs 5k to 20k tokens — those are heavy and less latency-sensitive. But cost is huge for us. We're targeting a sub-$0.0006 per token average if possible.
[01:10] Evan: To add, some of the longer jobs are batched offline and could be run in dedicated pools, but the short live interactions need low latency.
[01:20] Maya: Makes total sense. Two levers you mentioned are common: route long batch-y workloads to reserved/dedicated capacity and keep short low-latency ones on hosted with smaller models or quantized variants.
[01:34] Priya: What's the real delta for batching though? If we batch 16 short requests together what's the per-token drop?
[01:41] Liam: Rough numbers — for short 150-token requests, baseline hosted uncached per-token cost X (we discussed model variant pricing offline). Batching 16 can reduce per-token compute by ~25-35% depending on attention patterns and kernel efficiency. But the biggest wins come from KV/prefix caching for repeated context. If you're sending similar prefixes, the KV cache can reduce repeated compute by 40-60% on the cached prefix.
[02:09] Jared: When you say KV cache, is that Redwood-hosted or do we manage the cache in our VPC? We have strict data controls.
[02:18] Liam: Good question. For Redwood Hosted, KV cache lives in our runtime but is ephemeral and encrypted in transit. For Dedicated and Private, we can run caching within your VPC or on the reserved pool depending on deployment. The behaviors differ slightly — hosted is managed and fast to onboard; private gives you control over residency and encryption keys.
[02:40] Sofia: Encryption — you said encrypted in transit, what about at rest? We need KMS integration and customer-managed keys for anything persisted.
[02:47] Tara: We do support customer-managed KMS for Private deployments and dedicated with private control plane; for hosted we offer envelope encryption and we can discuss bring-your-own-key in some enterprise plans. I'll attach the exact KMS matrix after.
[02:58] Sofia: Also, logs — do you store raw prompts in logs? For compliance we need minimization and redaction options.
[03:06] Maya: By default audit logs include metadata and IDs; raw prompt storage depends on the retention settings and can be disabled or redacted. We'll share an audit log sample.
[03:15] Priya: Good. Back to economics — if we do a pilot, what's a realistic way to surface the per-token economics?
[03:22] Liam: Best pattern we've seen: start with a 2-week pilot where you route a small slice of production traffic or replay traces. We instrument token counts pre/post batching and simulate KV hits. We produce unit-econ breakdown: model cost, GPU compute, networking, and overheads.
[03:37] Priya: We can supply traces — though sometimes traces have PII; any recommendations?
[03:42] Maya: You can sanitize traces before sending. Alternatively we can run an in-situ pilot within your VPC/private deployment to avoid sending data offsite. That keeps data residency and security happy.
[03:53] Jared: How heavy is the private deployment lift? We don't want a month-long project.
[03:58] Liam: For our private on-prem package, typical timeline is 4-6 weeks for a fully air-gapped rollout; for VPC-hosted private control plane it's often 1-2 weeks if networking and IAM are ready. Dedicated reserved pools are quickest to enable if you can accept data routing to our dedicated infra.
[04:18] Evan: Cost-wise, if we choose dedicated reserved, how do upfront commits compare to hosted per-token?
[04:24] Maya: Roughly, dedicated reserved gives you a lower per-token compute rate because the GPU amortization is committed; hosted is pay-as-you-go and higher per-token but no upfront. We'll send a pricing table with concrete numbers for your token profiles.
[04:37] Sofia: SLA and fallbacks — if a reserved pool has an outage, what are the failover options? We need predictable behavior.
[04:44] Liam: We support automated fallback routing to compatible model variants in hosted tiers and cross-region replication for dedicated pools. We'll propose a canary/fallback SLO and an RTO/RPO outline for the pilot.
[04:57] Priya: One more — quantization. Our models are open: can you host quantized weights and does that change inference accuracy?
[05:05] Liam: Yes, runtime supports INT8/4 quantization profiles; the accuracy delta depends on model and task. We recommend running a quality regression on your eval set; Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles and we can run A/B. Quantization reduces GPU memory and boosts throughput which reduces per-token cost quite a bit.
[05:27] Evan: Any hard numbers for INT8 on 13B variants?
[05:31] Liam: Typical throughput improvement 1.8x-2.5x, token cost reduction around 30-45% for throughput-bound workloads. But accuracy checks are mandatory.
[05:44] Jared: Network egress — if we run private in our VPC and call smaller hosted models, is egress charged?
[05:51] Maya: If we route via Redwood-hosted endpoints there is cross-cloud egress — we'll include those estimates. For Private deployments within your VPC, egress is internal.
[05:59] Priya: Ok. For the pilot, we want to understand token mix sensitivity. Can you show per-token costs across three mixes — mostly short, mixed, and mostly long?
[06:08] Liam: Yep. We'll prepare a sensitivity sheet mapping per-token to batch sizes and cache hit rates. We'll include a scenario for adaptive batching (batch sizes vary based on queueing) and for prefix caching at 0%, 25%, 50%, 75% hit rates.
[06:24] Sofia: On SSO and RBAC — we need SAML SSO with SCIM, and granular role-based access to models and audit logs. Is that available?
[06:33] Tara: Yes. SAML + SCIM for user provisioning is supported in our enterprise console. RBAC covers model-level access and API key scoping. For Private we can integrate with your IdP directly.
[06:44] Sofia: And the audit trail — retention and export formats?
[06:47] Maya: Audit logs can be exported in JSON and kept for configurable retention. For enterprise we support longer retention windows and we can push logs to your SIEM via secure forwarders.
[06:58] Priya: What about reproducibility of results across model updates? We need pinned model versions for compliance.
[07:04] Liam: You can pin model versions in the deployment config and Redwood supports rollbacks. For hosted we publish model performance notes; Dedicated/Private gives you stronger version guarantees.
[07:15] Evan: Any case studies for bio or regulated workloads?
[07:18] Maya: We have a few anonymized examples. I'll include a short note about a genomics startup that used dedicated pools plus KV caching to cut inference spend by ~40% while keeping latency under their SLO.
[07:30] Jared: Ok next — price transparency. Can we get a line-itemed invoice for compute, storage, and support?
[07:36] Tara: Yes. Our billing can be broken out. For pilots we often provide a trial credit and then a usage report showing per-route and per-model breakouts.
[07:47] Priya: Timeframe — we have a budget window early January but need security review before kickoff.
[07:52] Maya: Proposed timeline: Redwood sends docs and unit-econ sheet by Thursday (Dec 10). Security deep-dive the following week (Sofia + Redwood security). Pilot kickoff target week Jan 4.
[07:59] Sofia: We'll need Redwood's SOC2 report and a network diagram before we sign off.
[08:04] Tara: We'll push the SOC2 pack and an anonymized network diagram; we can also run a short compliance checklist call.
[08:12] Priya: For the pilot traffic shaping, can we limit tokens per minute and signal if cost exceeds thresholds?
[08:18] Liam: Yes, we can configure rate limits and per-tenant cost alerts; Redwood Optimize can suggest batch thresholds. We can also route long jobs to a dedicated reserved pool automatically if thresholds are exceeded.
[08:31] Evan: Any specific API changes required to enable batching or cache hints?
[08:36] Liam: Minimal. There are headers/options to pass a request group id for affinity to cache and optional hints for expected sequence length. For streaming we also provide chunked responses.
[08:48] Maya: Let's recap and lay out action items.
[08:51] Maya: Items: Redwood sends unit-econ sensitivity, benchmarking notes for INT8 and batching, SOC2 + KMS docs, and a pilot SLO template. Aquifer will send sanitized traces and confirm pilot week.
[09:05] Priya: Sounds good. One last question — if after pilot numbers look good, what's commitment cadence for getting dedicated reserved capacity?
[09:12] Maya: Usually a short negotiation for a 3-12 month reserved pool; we size based on pilot throughput and provide a phased ramp. We'll include some commit tiers in the pricing packet.
[09:22] Jared: Great. Thanks everyone.
[09:24] Sofia: Thank you.
[09:26] Meeting ends.
